rows.label: Concept
rows.text: ## The story at a glance "The Half-Closed Eyes of the Buddha and the Slowly Sinking Sun" by Manjushree Thapa is a story about two ways of seeing the same country. A tourist guide spends a day showing a visiting teacher the Kathmandu the tourists buy — the Shangri-La of golden temples, smiling faces and timeless serenity — while the teacher keeps seeing what the brochure crops out: the polio-stricken child carried on…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Contrast: tourist's aesthetic gaze vs the reality of poverty and disability in Nepal.
The smile of the Buddha statue overlooks suffering — irony of spiritual tourism.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Trick 3: The Buddha's half-closed eyes (compassion) vs the sinking sun (fading hope) — unpack both title images for the symbolism marks.  ·  ## The characters worth an essay **The guide** is the story's compromise: not a villain but a working man selling the image his market pays for — and his discomfort in the poor household shows the performance is wearing thin even on its performer.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: ## The themes worth an essay **Two views of a country** — the central theme: the packaged East sold to visitors against the lived East endured by locals; the story asks who profits from the first and who pays for it. **Serenity and suffering** — the Buddhist image interrogated: is the half-closed gaze peace, or the luxury of not looking? **Tourism and its gaze** — the theme of representation: what the visitor is…  ·  ## NEB short answers, solved **Q. What does the tourist guide show the visitor? (2 marks)** A. The packaged Nepal: golden temples, ancient stupas, smiling faces and timeless serenity — the Shangri-La of the tourist trade. The story presents this as a selection rather than a lie: a real beauty curated to crop out the poverty beside it. **Q. How does the teacher's view differ from the guide's? (2 marks)** A.…

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. How do the two characters see Nepal differently? (3 marks) — tourist: aesthetic beauty; guide: real suffering behind the beauty.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ## NEB long answers, solved **Q. "The story contrasts the Nepal that is sold with the Nepal that is lived." Discuss. (8 marks)** A model answer builds the two Nepals with the story's own evidence: the guide's patter — stupas, smiles, timeless serenity — against the teacher's knowledge — the west, the hospital queues, the carried child — and stages the collision in the poor household scene, where the performance…

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## The plot, retold with an eye on its turns The setup is a guided day: the guide narrates the valley's glories in the language of the trade — the stupas and shrines, the "living museum", the smile of the people — and the story's first movement is the tourist's Kathmandu, polished and performed. Thapa writes the guide's patter with precision: it is not a lie exactly, but a selection, and the selection is for sale.…  ·  ## The devices, with evidence - **Contrast** — the story's engine: the tourist's golden Kathmandu against the teacher's Kathmandu of hospital queues and carried children; the performed smile against the endured day. - **Juxtaposition of images** — the title itself: the Buddha's half-closed eyes and the sinking sun set side by side so that serenity and decline illuminate each other; the pairing is the story's…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Two voices structure the story: the tourist sees postcard beauty; the Nepali guide sees poverty and suffering behind it — the double vision IS the theme.  ·  Trick 2: The tourist's exoticising gaze is critiqued — she consumes misery as scenery; collect two lines where her insensitivity shows.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q. What do the title's two images symbolise? (2 marks) — compassionate detachment (Buddha's eyes) and hope's decline (sinking sun).
